title: Installing a washing machine standpipe and trap
subtitle: The correct drain connection for a washing machine that prevents siphonage and backflow
excerpt: A washing machine drain hose pushed into a sink trap or loosely into a drain hole is a common source of foul smells, siphonage, and slow drainage. A properly installed standpipe with an integral trap provides a permanent, self-sealing drain connection. This is a 2-hour plumbing job requiring no specialist tools.
sourceNotes: BS EN 60335-2-7 on household washing machine installation requirements (drain height). Building Regulations Part H (Drainage and Waste Disposal) on standpipe height and trap requirements. Plumbworld and BES installation guides for standpipe fitting.

glossaryTerms.definition: A vertical length of 40 mm or 50 mm diameter pipe into which the washing machine drain hose is inserted. The standpipe terminates at the correct height and connects to a trap below, which provides an air seal against foul gas from the drain.
The unintended emptying of a trap by the suction created when water flows past its outlet. In a washing machine connection, siphonage can empty the trap seal and allow sewer gas to enter the room.

content.text: The drain hose supplied with most washing machines is designed to hook over a sink edge or push into a 40 mm pipe. Both methods are temporary solutions that eventually cause problems: the hose works loose during the spin cycle, or the sink trap is inadequate for the surge flow of a washing machine pump discharge and the water backs up. A
with an integral or adjacent trap is the permanent solution required by BS EN 60335-2-7.

The top of the standpipe must be between 600 mm and 900 mm from the floor. Below 600 mm, water from the drain can back-siphon into the machine. Above 900 mm, the machine pump has to push water up against too much head and the manufacturer's warranty may be voided.
The drain hose should loop up to the standpipe entry point without sharp kinks. A kink in the hose restricts flow and causes the pump to overwork.
Install a 40 mm P-trap at low level, connecting to the existing waste pipe in the wall or floor. Use a push-fit trap with a 75 mm seal depth to resist
Connect a vertical 40 mm plastic pipe (standpipe) rising to 700 mm height from the trap outlet. Clip to the wall with two pipe clips.
The top of the standpipe should be open (not capped). The machine drain hose sits into the open top, held in place by a retaining clip if supplied by the manufacturer.
Do not seal the drain hose into the standpipe: the gap between hose and pipe is intentional. It prevents siphonage by providing an air break at the inlet.
Test by running a rinse cycle and checking for leaks at the trap joints and for any water overflow from the standpipe top.

The standpipe trap should connect to a 40 mm or 50 mm branch that joins the household waste system above the main soil stack. Do not connect directly into a soil pipe for WC waste; connect to a dedicated branch for the utility room. If no branch is present, cut into the existing 40 mm under-sink waste pipe and install a swept branch connector.

rows.symptom: Drain hose pumps water but water runs back into the machine
rows.cause: The standpipe height is below 600 mm, allowing backflow when the pump stops
rows.fix: Extend the standpipe to bring the top to at least 600 mm from the floor. Check the machine's drain hose loop height matches the standpipe entry point.

rows.symptom: Foul smell from the area around the standpipe
rows.cause: The trap has dried out from a period of non-use, or the trap seal depth is insufficient for the surge flow
rows.fix: Pour a litre of water into the standpipe to refill the trap. If the smell persists immediately after a wash cycle, replace the trap with a deep-seal (75 mm) model.
